anchor: A Chieftain to the Highlands bound
note: Chieftain: the head of a Scottish clan. The Highlands are the mountainous north of Scotland.

anchor: Out spoke the hardy Highland wight
note: Wight: a person, a fellow. Hardy: tough and brave.

anchor: But for your winsome lady
note: Winsome: charming and engaging, pleasing to look at.

anchor: The water-wraith was shrieking
note: Water-wraith: a ghost or spirit of the water, whose cry was thought to foretell drowning.

anchor: And in the scowl of heaven each face
note: Scowl: a dark, angry frown.

anchor: Adown the glen rode armed men
note: Adown: down. Glen: a narrow valley.

anchor: Love has bliss, but Love has ruing
note: Ruing: sorrow, regret, feeling sorry afterward.

anchor: Longest stays, when sorest chidden
note: Chidden: scolded, rebuked with angry words.

anchor: Love’s wing moults when caged and captured
note: Moults: sheds feathers, as birds do.

anchor: Or the ringdove’s neck from changing
note: Ringdove: a wood pigeon whose neck feathers change color in the light.

anchor: So fair thy pensile beauty burns
note: Pensile: hanging down, as the evening star hangs low in the sky.

anchor: Sure some enamour’d orb above
note: Enamour’d: in love. Orb: a heavenly body, a star or planet.

anchor: Queen of propitious stars, appear
note: Propitious: favorable, bringing good luck.

anchor: Where, winnow’d by the gentle air
note: Winnow’d: blown through, stirred by a current of air.

anchor: Her silken tresses darkly flow
note: Tresses: long locks of hair.

anchor: Where Blake and mighty Nelson fell
note: Robert Blake and Horatio Nelson were great British admirals. Nelson fell in battle, and the song calls on sailors to follow them.
source: Encyclopædia Britannica, 11th ed. (1911), “Blake, Robert”, https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/1911_Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica/Blake%2C_Robert; Encyclopædia Britannica, 11th ed. (1911), “Nelson, Horatio Nelson, Viscount”, https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/1911_Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica/Nelson%2C_Horatio_Nelson%2C_Viscount

anchor: Britannia needs no bulwarks
note: Bulwarks: walls built for defense. Britannia is a name and picture of Britain as a woman.

anchor: Of Nelson and the North
note: In 1801 Nelson led a British fleet against the Danish fleet at Copenhagen, after Denmark and other northern powers joined a league against Britain.
source: Encyclopædia Britannica, 11th ed. (1911), “Copenhagen”, https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/1911_Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica/Copenhagen; Encyclopædia Britannica, 11th ed. (1911), “Nelson, Horatio Nelson, Viscount”, https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/1911_Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica/Nelson%2C_Horatio_Nelson%2C_Viscount

anchor: Like leviathans afloat
note: Leviathan: a huge sea monster, here a mighty warship.

anchor: It was ten of April morn by the chime
note: The Battle of Copenhagen was fought on the 2nd of April 1801, when the Danes resisted bravely but lost their fleet.

anchor: From its adamantine lips
note: Adamantine: unbreakable, hard as diamond. The “lips” are the cannon’s mouth.

anchor: Or in conflagration pale
note: Conflagration: a large destructive fire, here of burning ships.

anchor: Elsinore!
note: Elsinore is a Danish town on the narrowest part of the Sound, the strait between Denmark and Sweden.

anchor: On Linden, when the sun was low
note: The Battle of Hohenlinden was fought on 2 December 1800 near Munich. French troops under Moreau beat the Austrians. Hohen Linden means “high lime trees.”
source: F. T. Palgrave, The Golden Treasury (1861), Palgrave’s Notes, Poem 215, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/19221

anchor: The snow shall be their winding-sheet
note: Winding-sheet: the cloth wrapped around a dead body.

anchor: When first the fiery mantled Sun
note: Mantled: cloaked, covered as with a cloak.

anchor: On Calpe’s olive-shaded steep
note: Calpe is the old name for Gibraltar, the great rock at the southern tip of Spain, at the entrance to the Mediterranean.
source: F. T. Palgrave, The Golden Treasury (1861), Palgrave’s Notes, Poem 256, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/19221

anchor: Round the shore where loud Lofoden
note: Lofoden is a group of islands off northwest Norway, where a great whirlpool, the Maelstrom, was said to swallow whales.
source: F. T. Palgrave, The Golden Treasury (1861), Palgrave’s Notes, Poem 256, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/19221
